item.title: Solar power, from futurist speculation to business plan
item.description:
One mode of futurism is estimating the limits of a technology, without regard to what's currently feasible. Whether this is of any relevance to your own generation is another question.

Let's consider solar power. Ignoring current technology, it's easy to put a number on the maximum power output. The solar power at the Earth's distance from the sun is called the solar constant. It is 1.36 kW/m². The power on a square meter of the ground is less than that, because of the angle of incidence as well as the atmosphere.

The solar constant hasn't changed and technology has, so it's interesting to see how people have reacted to the same number throughout the history of technology. In this post I'll quote both Nikola Tesla and Elon Musk. We'll see that Tesla correctly recognized solar power as a long-term possibility, as well as why it was impractical in the short term.

From Musk all I really have is a Twitter thread where he does the arithmetic. But it's interesting to consider what has changed since Nikola Tesla's time, and how someone in Musk's generation may have recognized that it was the time to act on these calculations.

Nikola Tesla on the solar future

The Tesla quote is from a 1931 article called "Our Future Motive Power", which discusses solar power as one of many options.

Nature has provided an abundant supply of energy in various forms which might be economically utilized if proper means and ways can be devised. The sun's rays falling upon the earth's surface represent a quantity of energy so enormous that but a small part of it could meet all our demands. By normal incidence the rate is mechanically equivalent to about 95 foot pounds per square foot per second, or nearly 7300 horse power per acre of ground. In the equatorial regions the mean annual rate is approximately 2326 and in our latitudes 1737 horse power for the same area. By using the heat to generate steam and operating a turbine under high vacuum probably 200 horsepower per acre could be obtained as net useful power in these parts. This would be very satisfactory were it not for the cost of the apparatus which is greatly increased by the necessity of employing a storage plant sufficient to carry the load almost three-quarters of the time.

Tesla's number of 7300 horsepower per acre is approximately the solar constant.

Although Tesla is thinking of using sunlight as a source of heat for a steam engine, he goes on to note that we could instead use "photo-electric cells which may become, on this account, of practical importance in the future." Now we use photovoltaic cells, so that's one thing that has changed since his time.

The other is that with modern batteries, we can construct a "storage plant", as Tesla called it. If you keep reading the Tesla article, he seems to think storage would be unnecessary in the long term; apparently he thought his ideas for wireless power transmission would work across continents. But another scientist and futurist, J. B. S. Haldane, correctly identified storage as the key issue when discussing wind power in his 1924 book, where he wrote:

Even to-morrow a cheap, foolproof, and durable storage battery may be invented, which will enable us to transform the intermittent energy of the wind into continuous electric power.

Well, it took longer than that, with lithium-ion batteries becoming widespread in the '90s.

Elon Musk on the solar present

A 2024 Twitter thread:

Once you understand Kardashev Scale, it becomes utterly obvious that essentially all energy generation will be solar.

Also, just do the math on solar on Earth and you soon figure out that a relatively small corner of Texas or New Mexico can easily serve all US electricity.

One square mile on the surface receives ~2.5 Gigawatts of solar energy. That’s Gigawatts with a “G”. It’s ~30% higher in space. The Starlink global satellite network is entirely solar/battery powered.

Factoring in solar panel efficiency (25%), packing density (80%) and usable daylight hours (~6), a reasonable rule of thumb is 3GWh of energy per square mile per day. Easy math, but almost no one does these basic calculations.

The solar constant appears here as Musk's value in space (approximately; probably he meant that his ground value is 30% lower, which gives a closer match).

2024 is late, but Musk was early to solar power. In 2006, when the only Tesla car was the Roadster, he wrote that "the overarching purpose of Tesla Motors (and the reason I am funding the company) is to help expedite the move from a mine-and-burn hydrocarbon economy towards a solar electric economy".

This was timely not just because solar panels were getting cheap, but because of lithium-ion batteries. And not just for cars: Tesla (the company) was way ahead on stationary batteries for the electric grid. But that's a story for another post.

item.title: Twenty Minutes Into the Future: On Launching “Terminal Values”
item.description:
Cross-posted from Oblomovka.

It’s 4AM on a Monday morning. In a few hours, I’m supposed to be launching a new digital rights organisation at the Cypherpunk Congress, in Mumbai, India. I’m still in my pyjamas in San Francisco.

This part, at least, was somewhat planned. I told Mykola Siusko and Becca Creamer, the organisers, I had an important announcement, which I’d do by a remote video link. Everything else is a little improvised.

For a start, I sort of hate video presentations at conferences. It’s always a challenge to keep the energy up in a live audience when they pull up the giant screen, and someone gives their pre-recorded spiel. This is why, two hours earlier, I had decided to liven things up by announcing Terminal Values as a giant, glowing, disembodied head.

I am dignity incarnate.

A month previously, I 75% quit my job at the Filecoin Foundation. I’d spent the last five years funding and advising organisations who were building a decentralised vision of the Internet and Web. I left because I realised I was antsy to get back in the game. As you may have noticed, things are, in the year of our lord 2026, going down. But after five years of being heads-down in one ecosystem, I didn’t really have a strong grip of the lay of the land, and what needed to be done. I tagged along to the Global Free Speech Summit in Tennessee the day after I left my job to scope things out.

Late at night there, I ask my friend Farzaneh Badii: what is to be done? She’s an Iranian exile and human rights activist, who has spent the last years in the digital trenches, fighting for the open Internet at governance meetings and conferences: at ICANN, the IETF, the W3C, and other mysterious acronyms.

We start writing a list. The list starts at Velvet Taco, moves on to Robert’s Western World honkytonk, and ends at an absinthe bar on the edge of town. At some point, the items stop beginning with “Someone should…” and start reading “We should…”. Domains are bought. Plans are made.

I’ve done this before — launch an org — an inadvisable number of times. The most successful in this domain was plotting with Suw Charman-Anderson to start what became the Open Rights Group in the UK.

(I feel like we don’t convey enough how easy it is to start a thing, and how hard it is to end it once you start. For a procrastinator like me, it’s an excellent gee-up.)

And now I’m a floating head, astrally projected thousands of miles away by the Internet that isn’t just a vehicle for my beliefs, but the proof-of-possibility that forged my beliefs, trying to explain Terminal Values for the first time.

Terminal Values

The name: it comes from an essay Techdirt’s Mike Masnick commissioned from me, two years ago. It means that the values we fight for — the old-fashioned Internet idealism of a global network, free of surveillance and censorship, for everyone, by everyone — are ends in themselves. That’s the meaning of terminal values. That’s opposed to “instrumental values” — the values you pick to help you achieve other, nobler ends.

I wrote it because something kept bugging me about my strategy (as Director of Strategy) at EFF in the last decade.

Politics had been polarising over that time. The traditional “undivide and deconquer” tactic of civil libertarians was increasingly unviable. Previously, we would reach out across every political aisle to pull together a ragtag coalition of Internet freedom lovers. I’d cut my activist teeth pulling together a proto-net-neutrality coalition of “strange bedfellows” (as every press release we sent had headlined) which had included progressive gadflies MoveOn and the gunnier-than-the-NRA Gun Owners of America. The idea of an equivalent model campaign in the 2020s, featuring MAGAs and democratic socialists, or just Democrats and Republicans, living together, had become unthinkable.

So instead we started tailoring the arguments to each constituency. To progressives and libertarians, I talked about the dangers of geotracking when it could be used to expose users of Grindr in states with anti-gay laws, or visitors to abortion clinics. To the right and to marginalised communities, we connected their concerns about being silenced in mainstream social media to the importance of supporting alternatives to the social media giants. (To hear many of these arguments from that time, check out the podcast I hosted with Cindy Cohn, How To Fix The Internet.)

I believed then, and believe now, that this is a valid strategy — indeed, I don’t think any of us thought of it as a strategy at all, just as the obvious, only thing to do.

But we spent our time talking about what the Internet did for other causes, and not the principles behind the Internet itself. I believe these ideas are radical and liberatory in themselves, and worthy of consideration whether they improve the chances of other policies or not.

The Internet comes with its own ideas about liberty, just as the printing press did, like the steam engine did, and coinage did, like agriculture and religion before them. Absolute freedom of speech, absolute privacy, without gatekeepers or government surveillance, is a possibility realised by modern technology — but you only grasp its ramifications and its value when you feel its power and possibility thrumming through the machine in front of you. You don’t argue for a free press before you see and touch and use a printing press. Technology changes what we think of as freedom. Everyday politics often lags behind these changes, so a technological revolution explained in the terms of the systems of thought that preceded it will always miss something vital — and risk smothering it in its cradle.

So, somewhere along the way, I stopped arguing for the future the Internet makes possible, and started arguing merely for its present benefits. And the political operators we spoke to, more popular and confident than us, began using and modifying our arguments themselves, for a vision of technology that was biased, just a little bit, toward their political group. Free speech for me, but not for thee. Privacy and encryption — but with backdoors, just in case those other people are up to something.

Once again: I don’t think that was a bad approach at all. But it did have consequences. The most important one being: after ten years of not telling the stories and the dream, people simply forgot them. And a new generation grew up, feeling that there was something good buried in the network, but without history or context to understand what was possible, or that they were not alone in their dreams. They turned to more immediate politics, with bigger stories to tell.

I gently argued this in that 2024 article, but as I watched time move on, I felt it more and more. Farzaneh and other radical voices, still in the trenches, told me it was getting worse. There were either lone voices arguing for the fundamentals, from orgs like EFF and Fight for the Future, or more often no voices at all.

So: Terminal Values, reflecting its name, will go back to these basics: free speech, free software, free knowledge, free association; secure and private personal technology, under the direct control of its users, operable without borders, without censors, and without limitations. And we’ll present them as they should be: for everyone, not for what they do for one camp or another.

(And yes, it’s also a pun on terminal. Someone taught you what a terminal was, right?)

Twenty Minutes Into the Future

It’s hard to tell from 8,400 miles away, but I think my floating head did okay. We got donations and sign-ups, and people talked online. Mainly about the giant floating head, to be honest. The number one thing people said was “Hey, it’s like Max Headroom!”

This is great, because a movement needs an aesthetic, a look-and-feel, and a vibe. Max Headroom appeared in the Eighties, but prefigured a Nineties visual world of VR and neon. A Nineties style is perfect for the dreams of a better Internet. As the years move on, the Nineties has stopped being a weird Gen X side-alley, and started being a place of interest for curious new people to visit and adopt. There was a long while when we all desperately worked to avoid looking like we were stuck in the Nineties. Now, people wear those haircuts with pride. We’re going to lean into that.

The number one thing I want to pluck from the Nineties is its orientation to the future. From our viewpoint a quarter-century on, the Nineties future was imminent, promising, and changeable. Max Headroom lived twenty minutes into the future, because he embodied what people felt was coming in the run-up to the millennium, far too fast to stop.

I feel — against the temporary pessimism of the present age — that we are in such a moment again. We want Terminal Values to argue for causes and actions that sound semi-ridiculous right now, but in six months’ time will seem prescient — or hopelessly dated.

(Also, Terminal Values abbreviates to “TV”, and the number of Nineties-themed TV puns we can make is nearly infinite.)

Let me give you a concrete example, which shows, I think, how TV can complement and extend existing campaigns. The brilliant Thorin Klosowski wrote a piece for EFF this week called “Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)”. He skewers the new rewriting of norms that tech companies are pursuing whereby one person gets to “consent” to the recording and surveillance of everyone else in a video meeting, or private conversation. I urge you to read it — as if you haven’t already read enough today.

TV’s role in this is to “yes, and” these points — and point to the future conundrum. It’s terrible for one person to consent to hand over everybody’s conversation to a third party. But we have to work out a way for an individual to be able to use their own devices to interpret, translate, absorb or simplify the conversations they are part of, using technology that they fundamentally control.

Commercial AI and hardware that hand all that data off to companies, and thence to hackers and governments, can’t be the answer. But for digital technology to play its starring role in augmenting us, whether by compensating for our disabilities or by extending our temporary limits, we have to work out a way for it to safely and transiently partake or share in what we are doing and thinking. That doesn’t weaken privacy: it reaffirms the personal and private decision-making that privacy is intended to protect (what, in the 2024 article, I termed “cognitive liberty”).

Should that point be crammed into a piece about the rapidly changing mores of conversation recording, and the regulations around it? Probably not without weakening it. But somebody has to make that point — about the devices and tools we should be building, and that will exist, twenty minutes into the future. That’s our job.

“Open” Means Open to Everything — and Everyone

As I’ve talked about before here, there’s a valid strategy for technology-using activists which involves diligently avoiding the use of tech that does not accord with one’s values.

TV’s approach is that nothing technological is alien to us. Our aim is to experiment with technology, in order to see what might happen twenty minutes into the future, and to see what new opportunities and values might emerge from it — and how to mitigate its dangers. If you don’t use it, you can’t understand it, or talk about it.

We’re also determined to talk with any community, including any political community. Every group of thinkers can and should get their policies around the future in order. Some will reject us: I’ve had conversations, for instance, with the representatives of dictatorships, groups of authoritarian communists, and right-wing ethnonationalists. They have rarely gone particularly well. But it’s up to them to reject us, and it’s up to us to make the case for freedom.

If You’re Explaining, You’re Winning

There’s an old slogan in political activism that I first heard from Fred von Lohmann: “If you’re explaining, you’re losing.”

I think this is true for 90% of the work of achieving political goals. But sometimes, you just have to tell the bigger story, complicated and subtle though it may be.

We want to free all of our allies in this fight from having to do all the explaining, so they can go straight to winning.

Policy advocates shouldn’t have to constantly re-explain the history that allowed us to know that DRM is a bad idea, that closed security is no security, that network censorship leads to network fragility, and so on. Freed from the need not to explain, we’ll try to spell out the fundamentals, radical though they may be — and do this not just to the wider public, but to (sometimes shocked) policymakers in the venues where these fundamental points cannot easily be made by those at the negotiating table.

My favourite moments in tech activism — like Cory Doctorow blogging from the Broadcast Protection Discussion Group, or anti-software-patent activists paddling into Strasbourg to argue against restricting technological ideas — come from dedicated, knowledgeable technologists walking into venues where their ideas are almost certain to be misunderstood or rejected. There, they clearly, repeatedly, and sincerely articulated a complex, unsexy, technically challenging and radically honest viewpoint. Ultimately, they prevailed. The broadcast flag was rejected; the software patent directive was thrown out. Sometimes you have to explain to win.

First they sail at you, then you win.

Photo: Alberto Barrionuevo, CC BY-ND 3.0 ES.

What Now and How Much

So what will Terminal Values do in an average month? Well, as we speak, Farzaneh is en route to the IETF, arguing for the values encoded in the network’s protocols. I’m cutting explainer videos, and trying to get to the bottom of what the hell happened in the UK since I left. I’ve been speaking to human rights activists eager to find private ways to use AI — and connecting with AI startups who are already getting a knock on the door from government agencies, keen to sweep up your conversations. There’s more than that. I doubt any month is going to be average for the next few years.

Where will the money come from? The Open Rights Group was started with a pledge of five pounds a month from its founding members. I’ve always been a fan of monthly, individual donations: you can vote with your money, and you can pay what you can.

That said, Terminal Values is barely two weeks old. I can’t even ask you for that money, because we don’t yet have the business account. (You can give us crypto, though. You guys never worry about that stuff!)

TLDR: Join Me

If you’ve read this far, I hope you already like the cut of Farzaneh’s and my jib. You probably have some objections or concerns about our approach because you’re thoughtful and view every argument critically, plus our core demographic is absolute pains-in-the-arse like you. You’ll also be curious about the nitty-gritty of the positions we’ll be advocating.

Shorter, less personal pieces and more detailed policy analysis are coming. I just couldn’t wait any longer to tell you, reader, because I’m more excited about the future than I have been in a decade.

All I can ask right now is that you keep track of us, and what we’re doing. I’ll continue to post updates here, but what would help the most is if you’d join our Signal announcement list, or our mailing list. We plan to livestream the revolution — having regular check-ins where we don’t just explain our approach, but challenge you to tell us what to think.

The giant floating head compels you!

Giant open source floating head, that is: https://github.com/dannyob/obs-lsd



Discuss

item.title: Visualizing the Difficulty of AI Alignment
item.description:
Epistemic status: Low, but I hope to be wrong in interesting ways

As a non-computer scientist-scientist[1] I find it hard to think about the varying perspectives on Artificial Intelligence alignment difficulty. To make this more intuitive I invoke the 3D surface of a fitness landscape like structure as a visual representation.[2]

The AI Safety Landscape

AI safety is thought to be largely pre-paradigmatic, although of the current views AI safety perspectives there are noticeable camps, and within each there is wide variation. It is also rapidly evolving as more information comes out about their behavior that allows us to update.

Previous work categorizing these has focused on specific technical approaches as well as their feasibility.

Here I think of ‘alignment’ loosely, here it is represented as any mind that would not cause extinction (or an s-risk) while also having substantial power, this contrasts with misalignment which would lead to extinction (or an s-risk).

To simplify this I condense these to five main camps represented by their arguably most prominent opinion havers:

Although I agree that P(doom) is a Dumb Meme it is used here more as a heuristic for parsing levels of concern around AI. For more of their specific positions here are my references: Yann LeCun, Paul Christiano[3], Eliezer Yudkowsky[4], Daniel Kokotajlo [5]and Roman Yampolskiy.

Visual Representation

In my mind’s eye, the alignment landscape manifests similarly to a fitness landscape.[6]

A fitness landscape is typically used to display the relationship between genotypes and reproductive success. Here I try to replace those axes with variance between digital minds contrasted with the difficulty to reach those minds using current methods. This difficulty space then intersects with a higher ‘alignment’ space where everything outside of this space is misaligned[7] (the total space would manifest as 4D) of holding anything remotely desirable to humans, here they are represented by red dashed lines and gestured to as ‘alignment’.

There are likely many areas with difficult or easy places to reach without alignment intersecting, but here I try to focus on firstly what I think-these-thinkers-think about the alignment space as it runs into the capability space and secondly, how easy it is to navigate there.

Capabilities

Here I think of fairly primitive AI minds are thought to be primarily neither aligned nor misaligned (I think of them more through the simulators lens). But, as AIs are trained and gain capabilities, they also gain the potential to be aligned/misaligned and distort the alignment space. This space is dependent on the training methods, and is somewhat tied to capabilities space.

Maybe as they are trained the surface sinks into misalignment or rises to alignment.

Important Subfactors:

Movement:

Through manipulations and some types training you can move models through mindspace without robustly changing (most) capabilities.

Verification:

How can we know where an alignment zone is? Is it possible to easily verify what is aligned and what is not? There could be vast foggy areas that surround what is verifiable or just a null set if we have no reasonable ways to verify anything about alignment state.

Steepness:

Steep slopes represent places that have a locally high change in difficulty and more effort to hill climb but is still navigable, a cliff represents something that is basically non-navigable with current methods.

Intensely steeps slopes may require different methods to climb than less steep slopes, such as using RLHF for small slopes versus Constitutional AI for a somewhat steeper slope.

Navigation:

It may be hard to know where the model is in this larger space, as well as what to do to move in a more aligned direction. Movement through this likely requires some form of verification mechanism to distinguish between what is ‘aligned’ and what is not.

Visualization for the 5 camps:

Yann LeCun: Alignment by default

When I think of Yann’s perspective and many tool AI thoughts I think of a global alignment attractor.

As you train a basin forms, and in difficulty space the model is pulled towards an aligned state without much extra effort. He also has gestured to it as an engineering problem, which would likely make the space flatter with some regions of alignment that just need the model to be pushed there. The regions of alignment are likely also plentiful and easier to find in the larger space.


Paul Christiano: Prosaic Alignment

When I think of Paul’s perspective I think of prosaic alignment and the need to use some resources to navigate to some of these harder-to-reach aligned places. Some RLHF, Constitutional AI, Scalable oversight, and other methods should be sufficient to control. If no alignment work is done the default is likely misalignment.


Daniel Kokotajlo: Alignment via controllability and elicitation

When I think of Daniel’s perspective I think of a steep hill that is hard to hill climb, there may be ways to layer controllability and to elicit useful work from unaligned AIs to move into the aligned space. The space is hard to navigate but through rigorous checking and trustworthy automated research as well as applying other preemptive anti-scheming techniques it may be possible to reach an aligned state.


Yudkowsky: Agent Foundations

For Yudkowsky I think of an aligned state as a plateau, nearby there are few indications of ways to reach it, with current training methods or even comparable approaches. Unless there are extreme breakthroughs in alignment methods it does not seem tractable anytime soon.

Roman Yampolskiy: Impossibility

To someone like Roman there are few to no approaches that can navigate to aligned states. With current methods and approaches aligned states exist as non-intersecting within the possible variation of these trained minds.

What does the larger space look like?

Would it be smooth, rugged, are there large attractors? I have no idea, since we are still pre-paradigmatic for alignment science this is only speculation.

Anthropic’s perspective and where (I think) we are now

In 2023 Chris Olah posted some graphs and perspectives on Anthropic’s thoughts about the difficulty of AI safety. I feel as if we can now reflect on those (as of Nov. 11, 2026).

Thus far have likely have spent >$100 million on alignment, with some progress. It does seem that some models are more aligned, (such as Fable vs. Astra).[8]

Given the RSI speedup and alignment still being not even close to solved, I personally have updated to alignment likely being harder than P vs. NP, Chris Olah’s ‘pessimistic safety view’ seems to be more accurate than that safety isn’t a problem.

I feel as if we are somewhere here. Easy alignment does not seem to be true, and it seems we are moving far too fast to reasonably solve this by the time superintelligence arrives.

  1. ^

    I am a Geologist subject outsider looking inwards.

  2. ^

  3. ^

    The 11% comes specifically from his post discussing his positions on doom.

  4. ^

    I place this above 90% because if Anyone Builds It Everyone Dies although to my knowledge Yudkowsky does not like P(doom) as a way of representing concern.

  5. ^

  6. ^

  7. ^

    In my depiction alignment space is its own thing that occasionally intersects with mindspace, where exactly it intersects seems to be thought different by each researcher, which is also part of the depiction.

  8. ^

    arguably

item.title: Trying to understand that compute multiplier graph
item.description:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video has a graph. It shows four models; I think dot 1 = Claude 3.5, dot 2 = Claude 4, dot 3 = Mythos, arrowhead = unreleased model.

The graph provided doesn't have any numbers on the Y axis. In this post I'll explain why I think the Y axis lines most likely represent a 10x jump each, and so the point at the end of the graph represents about a 30000x CM (i.e. Anthropic can currently pretrain models at the same quality with 1/30000th of the compute it needed in 2024). I'm pretty unsure about this though and it could plausibly be much higher or much lower. Keep in mind that this graph is only about pretraining and doesn't say anything about post-training.[1]

Without extra context, it's hard to say how much the compute has actually been multiplied: if each Y gridline is 1.1x the total multiplier would be about 1.53x; if each Y gridline is 10x the total multiplier would be about 30000x. (It's not clear to me why the last point is an arrowhead instead of a dot - maybe it's supposed to be their guess of what the compute multiplier will end up at for their latest pretraining run?)

What people in the IPO roadshow video say about compute multipliers

Sam McCandlish said (while that graph was displayed):

It’s how we serve models to customers and how we use Claude at scale internally. By training what we believe to be the most efficient models, we can do more of all these things with the same amount of compute. It’s also how we drive down costs, both for customers as well as our own underlying costs. We’re accelerating these efficiency gains through our research process. Our pace of discovery is speeding up, and a lot of that acceleration comes from Claude itself.

Tom Brown said:

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover.

Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4X compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model, or you can use those 100 physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would’ve previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that’s hard to replicate: they build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack.

We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We believe this combination of smart investments, breakthrough research, and the improving capabilities of Claude have put Anthropic in a leading position among the frontier labs.

Krishna Rao (CFO) said:

As Tom described, there are two drivers of this efficiency.

[...] The second is compounding compute multipliers, which have scaled our total effective compute significantly faster than our physical capacity. You can see this in our financial results. Over the last six quarters, we grew revenue by more than 45X, while compute and infrastructure costs grew only 10X. A more than 4X improvement in revenue per dollar of compute.

What is a CM?

From a deposition, a pretraining researcher explains what CMs are a bit better than the roadshow video:

Q. What do you mean by "makes the model dumber"?

A. Um, so the way that we normally define this is we -- because there's a notion of the compute efficient frontier. We're given a fixed budget of compute. There's an optimal way to train your model and an optimal loss you'll achieve on your objective function.

Um, so we can use this as a measuring stick comparing various models. So, for example, um, if you made the model much dumber, it might shift it down so as if you only had half as much compute to train that model.

Working backwards to estimate the actual compute multipliers

If we can estimate the CM from Claude 3.5 to Claude 4, we can work out where the rest of the points on the graph should be based on that. Here I try to estimate that number very roughly.

Model codename reference

We know the codenames from this filing, and some of the compute numbers from this graph.

Codename

Model

Training compute

junior

Unreleased model from mid-2022

4.2e24 FLOPs

finch

Stopped pretraining run from late 2022[2]


lark

Claude 1 (released March 2023)

1.6e25 FLOPs

eagle

Claude Instant (released March 2023)


eagle2

Claude Instant 1.1

2.0e24 FLOPs

tern

Claude 2 (released August 2023)


teal

Claude 3 Opus (released March 2024)


dove

Claude 3.5 Sonnet (released June 2024)


I believe lark is approximately finch but without training data from LibGen or PiLiMi, which hurt performance. I believe tern (Claude 2) was likely the same architecture as lark, and possibly continued pretraining on lark. Teal was almost certainly a fresh pretrain and a new architecture.[3]

Estimating Claude 1.0 -> Opus 3 CM

Claude 1 was pretrained with 1.6e25 FLOPs. We don't know how many FLOPs Claude 3 had, but it probably had around the same number of parameters as Claude 1 ("Lark [Claude 1] is actually too big, so Teal [Claude 3 Opus] will likely not be that much larger") but with much more data and a better architecture.

This graph[4] from an internal presentation shows that the actual amount of compute used to train Claude 1.0 was about 1.6e25 FLOPs. Extrapolating that graph to when Opus 3 pretraining finished would give 7.4e25 FLOPs. For various kinda complicated reasons[5] I think this is too high and it's actually more like ~4e25 FLOPs. So Opus 3 had ~2.5x the pretraining compute as Claude 1.0.

To calculate the 1.0 -> Opus 3 CM correctly we'd have to know how good 1.0 would be if we scaled it up to use as many FLOPs as Opus 3. We don't know that, but if you extrapolate based on how Llama3 scaled, you get that it would take 13x to 32x the compute. (Various other measures I tried roughly lined up with that too.) In other words, Opus 3 was as good as scaling up Claude 1.0 13x to 32x, but only took 2.5x the compute.

So 20 / 2.5 = 8x CM in the year between Claude 1.0 and Opus 3. That's an average of 1.005713 CM per day, so if we assume the rate of progress was the same for the 8 months between Claude 3.5 and 4 that's a 4x CM.

Estimating from individual CMs

There are multiple sources of pretraining compute multipliers: better pretraining data, a better training process that requires less tokens for the same capabilities, and better architectures.

For data quality related CMs:

  • "MMLU is too noisy to measure anything less than 1.1CM"
  • A 1.5x CM is insanely high (and maybe wrong?)
  • A 2x CM is so high it's assumed that there must have been accidental training on test data

So a normalish CM is maybe around 1.2? And maybe there'd be a few of them between model releases? Maybe we'll have ~6 ~1.2x CMs or ~4 ~1.3x CMs, for a ~3x CM between Claude 3.5 and Claude 4. I'm not sure if that's reasonable?

Working out the rest of the data points

If we assume a 3x CM for Claude 3.5 to Claude 4, then the grid lines are about 10x apart. 3x seems roughly reasonable given my estimates above, and it would make sense for the gridlines to be 10x apart each. Here's a widget Claude made where you can try different values for that first step, and see what that implies.

If you use try a CM of 5x for the first step it implies a total CM of ~3.3M and 10x would imply ~2.1B. Those would be absurdly and unreasonably large, so the first step CM is probably in the 3-4 region.

What the graph means

Keep in mind that you can improve pretraining performance on code just by changing the data mix (swapping out non-code documents for code documents). That would improve performance on code to the detriment of non-code. Anthropic has always had a lot of focus on making models good for coding, but I think it's fair to assume that they've been tilting the data mix more towards code since Claude 3.7 Sonnet (released February 2025) which was released alongside Claude Code. I doubt this skews the graph too much though.

Conclusion

Let me know if you have any questions! I'd love it if Anthropic was more transparent here; it seems valuable for them to communicate about the rate of progress in AI development.

  1. ^

    This makes it less useful for understanding RSI dynamics, since task-based RL is very important for model performance at model R&D.

  2. ^

    This transcript strongly implies that the only reason it was stopped was because Anthropic's lawyers advised that it should be stopped (presumably due to copyright concerns).

  3. ^

    This seems pretty clear to me, some evidence is that Claude 3 models use a different tokenizer than earlier ones.

  4. ^

    I think that graph is just pretrain compute, but it's not entirely clear to me. This doesn't matter too much though, since we only actually need the number for lark which I guess probably had >99% of compute spent on pretraining.

  5. ^

    I might explain this in a later post

item.title: Wargames inform present policy, not future incident response
item.description:
In January 2024, Ryan Greenblatt and Buck Shlegeris posted "Catching AIs red-handed." This post got on "Best of LessWrong" in 2025, and in December of last year Buck Shlegeris commented on it explaining that he was disappointed it did not lead to more follow-up research. I upvoted the post at the time of the review and think it is representative of the kind of concrete analysis the community values.

As it happens, it turned out to be remarkably prescient and near-term-relevant for a theorypost: just this August 2026 we, in fact, got to see what happens when AI companies "catch their AIs red-handed". The parties who wrote the post were, additionally, some of the very people involved in investigating the Hugging Face incident.

I definitely respect these researchers, but I struggle to imagine a means through which their analysis could have been useful for triaging those incidents. While it seems possible that publishing research like this is what put Redwood in a position to be called upon to investigate in the first place, the piece is just a long and abstract discussion about how (for example) if you catch an AI scheming, it is less likely to succeed (emphasis not mine):

In this post, we’ll discuss a crucial dynamic related to risk from scheming models. Suppose your model is trying to exfiltrate its weights or hack the datacenter or cause some other difficult-to-reverse bad outcome. (We’ll refer to all of these as the model “escaping”, because escape is linguistically convenient and is a good description of many of these difficult-to-reverse bad outcomes.) Our claim: once you’ve caught your models red-handed trying to escape, the situation changes substantially, in ways that are bad for the schemer’s chances of success.

And how, if you catch one of your AIs trying to escape, you should look for other AIs trying to escape:

Proliferation is where you try to capitalize on one example of AIs attempting to escape to find a diverse set of examples of AIs attempting to escape.

In the most simple case, this looks like trying to find nearby inputs that still result in an AI attempting an escape.

But more complex proliferation might be possible, because a serious escape attempt probably involves a substantial (>5) number of AI actions; in particular, actions from multiple different instances of AIs with access to different information and affordances. We try to make this be the case by implementing security measures that make bad actions impossible without many AIs collaborating.

People doing "alignment research" make a lot of these types of posts, essentially designing and juggling abstractions for alignment as a topic. I don't really understand what the theory of action for this work is supposed to be. I don't think it's harmful to do this analysis per se, and I don't think it's being done poorly or in bad faith, but there just doesn't seem to be much point. It reminds me of attending "cybersecurity" courses in university and listening to lectures about the CIA triad.

There are essentially two possible outcomes when you're speculating about "what to do" in response to future misalignment incidents:

  • Option A is that the post is just wrong or confused, either because its reasoning is bad or because it uses a completely wrong frame. Mostly alignment researchers get it wrong, because it's hard to do this kind of analysis well years in advance; any group of people would get it wrong.
  • Option B is that your analysis is right, but useless. Because by the time you get the chance to act on it, you're going to have much more direct evidence about what's going on, which obviates the need for the analysis in the first place. Your suggestions will sound stupid and circular no matter how prescient they are at the time, and the primary concerns of the people dealing with the problem are going to be whatever practical details are involved with doing the digital forensics.

This post, one of the lucky ones, seems to lie in the latter, fortuitous case. Did suggesting that we ought to "question the model and run experiments on it in the context where it misbehaved" inform any of OpenAI's investigations? How about "rerunning improved monitoring over past logs"? I hope someone reminded the safety team to test whether newly trained models do the same thing in a similar circumstance. They might not have thought of that!

The nearest actually useful analogue to this kind of analysis I can think of is wargames. With wargames, the reason they're useful, when they're useful, is that they inform present decisions on military policy. As an example I like, "AI 2040" is a wargame, yes, but it's a wargame for the purpose of generating a series of policy proposals, which are helpfully advertised on the website. It's hard for posts like the above to reach that bar when the content is so abstract, when it seems to be focused on advising people in the future rather than people in the present, and when (as far as I am aware) people who could be in a position to make policy decisions at the labs don't read this type of stuff anyways.



Discuss

item.title: A digital security checklist for the AI age
item.description:
We’re going to see huge, foundational cybersecurity attacks given the rapid rise in AI capabilities. Having worked in hostile environments, I’ve thought a lot about physical and digital security over the years. While you may not be personally targeted, or doing dangerous work, your data is undoubtedly leaked somewhere, and the digital providers you use—for email, banking, social media, etc.—are more and more likely to get hacked.

item.title: Protesting For AI Regulation
item.description:
There was an AI protest day today, with parallel protests around the world, and our family went to the Boston one:

I'm not really a protest person: normally I share my views in writing. But while there's been a lot of writing on the internet about the risk that AI gets us all killed (some of it from me), this can't be an internet-only thing. Way too few people are taking seriously the risk that OpenAI, Anthropic, and others are rapidly building something that could actually cause human extinction. A protest is a literal demonstration that people care, and it expands visibility to the general public.

We talked with the kids about whether they wanted to come, or whether I should take them somewhere while Julia went to the protest. All three did want to come, which makes sense: they've been hearing us talk about this at the dinner table and with friends for months, and the risk impacts them at least as much as it does us.

We painted some signs:

Clementine was not helpful:

Mine was a bit on the long side:

The crowd was mostly students, but there were also a lot of people I recognized from Boston EA meetups. Favorite sign: an "If You Can't Steer Don't Race", painted by someone I'd run into at LessOnline.

It was nominally a protest demanding a US–China treaty that bans more powerful AI until it can be done safely, but in practice it was a much more high level protest around the "slow down AI", "regulate AI", "AI bad", "RSI will get us killed", "AI companies irresponsible" cluster. If you hadn't seen the website, I don't think you'd have known about the treaty; no one mentioned it.

We alternated between a series of chants (quickly taught over the megaphone) and short speeches. The speeches included points I strongly supported (this is urgent, risks include extinction, safety regulation is a normal part of industry) and others I didn't (datacenter water use, it's wrong to make a technology that takes jobs, general scope insensitivity) but building a coalition of people who want to push the AI lever towards "slower" is fundamentally how a political movement has to work. I did stay quiet during a few chants, though, and if there's a way to avoid prudence in the face of superintelligence becoming partisan that seems very important.

Overall it was uncomfortable, and not really my thing, but I think it's important, liked being in a group of people pushing policy in a good direction, and would go again.

(More in this "online LW-ish person goes to an AI protest" genre: philh, Quadratic Reciprocity.)

Comment via: facebook, mastodon, bluesky

item.title: The Oldest Text in the Training Data
item.description:
What is the oldest text in Claude’s training data? Claude was trained on a non-trivial fraction of everything humans have ever written down. That includes the things you’d expect, like books and research papers. But it also includes microfilm archives, transcribed Betamax tapes, Donald Trump’s prenups, ancient scrolls and Harry Potter fanfiction. It’s a weird library.

So what is the oldest text in Claude's training data? It mostly depends on what we mean by "text". Here are some candidates:

The Epic of Gilgamesh

The Epic of Gilgamesh is considered the world's oldest written "great work of literature"; the earliest versions of it were written in 2100 BC in Sumer. The Sumerians did a fair amount of writing. Their medium was clay tablets. These tablets were designed to endure a few seasons of the Mesopotamian weather; this turned out to generalize well, and instead of surviving for a few years, they survived for millennia. Gilgamesh was lost in the sands of Iraq for a while, but was eventually dug up by European archeologists. The scholar who first translated the Epic to English got so excited by it that he took all of his clothes off and ran around the English museum shouting "I am the first man to read that after more than two thousand years of oblivion."

In the 1980s and 90s, scholars digitized many of the dug-up clay tablets. The museums would scan the tablets in normal office scanners and fax them to Assyriologists to phonetically transliterate. Those transliterations were somewhat lossy, so the major Mesopotamian scripts were eventually encoded in the Unicode system. Some of the largest Unicode characters come from Sumerian. E.g.:

𒐫 - is the character for the number 32,400

𒈙 - likely means rival kings or a battle between kings.

Each one of these is a single unicode character! They are great when you are doing QA or trying to make a website really ugly.

Anyways, Claude knows those languages well. In particular, it knows the Epic of Gilgamesh very well and can recite it more or less line by line in both Akkadian Unicode and in English.

Kushim’s Tablet

The Epic of Gilgamesh is famous for being good and interesting, not just for being old. There are many Sumerian texts that are far older. The Sumerian writing system was developed to keep track of debt and help with commodity logistics. It took them about 700 years to realize that writing was a universal information encoding system. They then started using it to keep track of love songs, jokes and epic stories.

The oldest texts are accounting entries from the administrative archives of Uruk, written between 3400 and 3000 BC, ~5000 years before the "current year of our Claude". We can’t say which tablet is the very oldest: they are dated by archaeological layer and handwriting style, so each one comes with a centuries-wide confidence interval. The most famous of them is the "Kushim Tablet".

The "Kushim Tablet" says something like: "exchange 29,086 measures of barley, 37 months, Kushim’s final account". Kushim is likely the name of the person who received the barley. We believe that Kushim turned the barley into beer. What else would you do with so much barley? Conservatively, this much barley is equivalent to about 900 cans of beer a day. From this, we can infer that Kushim was likely a very chill guy.

Claude can quote the "Kushim Tablet" in Sumerian Unicode. The tablet is definitely in the training data.

The Cone Token

Writing in Mesopotamia evolved from an older accounting system made of clay tokens. Each token stood for one unit: a cone was a small measure of grain, a sphere was a big measure of food. E.g., if you owed someone 23 measures, the record was three cones and two spheres (10s). The oldest tokens are about 10,000 years old. The tokens predate cities or the wheel.

At some point, ancient accountants started sealing the tokens inside of envelopes made from clay, a way to lock the information in a tamper-proof way. This method had one problem: you couldn’t check what was inside an envelope without smashing it. So the accountants pressed the tokens into the wet surface before sealing them in. Eventually someone noticed that the dents made the tokens redundant. This is where Mesopotamian text comes from.


When you press a cone into wet clay you get a small wedge. That wedge became the sign for "1"; this is what it looks like in Unicode: "𒁹". Claude knows the "𒁹" character very well, so the oldest text in Claude’s training data might be the cone token (or at least some evolution of it). Interestingly, writing began when we turned tokens into text. Claude reads by turning text into tokens.




Discuss

item.title: On the Brutality of Amdahl's Law
item.description:
Following my 3-week visit to Berkeley as described here and featured by ACX here, I told various people I would write in detail why I didn’t stick around to work in AI safety. In this post, I will dance around one object-level disagreement with AI safety and rationalists: why I no longer believe in explosive world transformation due to ASI. There will eventually be follow-up pieces on more object-level arguments and meta-level arguments against AI safety, but I prefer for this post to be mostly self-contained and not explicitly about AI safety.

When I worked in theoretical physics research, I was constantly reminded that if I were just that much smarter and had read that many more papers, I would be able to make the right connection to solve the problem. You are always the bottleneck; it’s always a skill issue. So if you’ve spent the bulk of your conscious life honing your ability to manipulate the pure abstraction of math and computer code, it is staggering to watch the problems you wrestled with for months or years get blown away in hours. You are left wondering how quickly all of the other problems in the world will be resolved - all of disease perhaps? Why not all of biology? Why not all the secrets of the universe?

In December 2025 when Claude Code + Opus 4.5 first made agents feel extremely useful, I was concerned about the job market being obliterated, so I took out “insurance” on rapid-onset white-collar unemployment. Thankfully, those predictions about increasingly capable agents causing rapid economic and labor transformation have been very wrong.

And so the question is, why? Why does the world largely look the same outside of highly verifiable domains like software engineering and math, and even in software engineering, why are there still millions employed? Why are models which can beat humans on nearly all benchmarks and are provided at unbelievably low prices not causing large economic shockwaves?

If I had to summarize my current perspective on AI in a single sentence, it would be that “the world is far too slow” to see the high double-digit or more economic growth and seismic transformations in the economy as predicted by various essays from the rationalist blogo-instituto-sphere.

Amdahl’s Law

I suspect the reason I’ve felt less “capabilities whiplash” than my peers is that a lot of my experience is in experimental science where how smart you are is often not the actual bottleneck. To illustrate how enormous speedup in one component does not translate to enormous broader speedup due to other bottlenecks, let’s make a simple model:

If you have a process with some number of steps to be completed sequentially, each with rate i (ie each step takes time 1/to complete), your total rate is given by

If you send every rate but one to infinity, you are still left with

This is almost a trivial statement - your overall process is rate-limited by the slowest step, but it can be easily forgotten as you watch individual rates arc hyperexponentially upwards:

From the new METR report

More realistically, suppose you have some hierarchy of rates

where r₀ = a is the slowest and each successive rate is b times faster than the previous. The total rate of this hierarchy is

If you send the first m bottleneck rates to infinity, entirely eliminating each bottleneck, the new rate is

The point is that in hierarchically bottlenecked systems, even infinite speedup of the bottleneck results in a constant factor aggregate speedup. In order to see exponential aggregate speedup, you need explosive improvement at the current bottleneck over and over again. Overall progress is often brutally suppressed by this interplay between bottlenecks.

If during each time window you focus all of your efforts on accelerating the current bottleneck to ~infinity (or really just far beyond the next bottleneck or two), you see constant factor speedup. Repeated infinite individual factor speedup yields only exponential aggregate speedup.

To see diminishing returns, the intelligence curve need not flatten out; you just have to hit some other bottleneck. And so the question as it pertains to AI causing disruption in the world (for better and worse) is not “where is intelligence the rate-limiting step?” but “when intelligence becomes free, instant, and near-omniscient, what is the new rate-limiting step?” In computer science, this speedup analysis is known as Amdahl’s law and is used for understanding the limits of parallelism, but variants of it appear all across science.

Is Intelligence the Bottleneck?

I suspect the most common objection to the above analysis is that I am failing to imagine what ASI can accomplish. Instead of trying to abstractly rebut this, let’s look at a banal example of fairly bounded speedups even when you have access to ASI:

You’re the manager of a widget factory, and for some reason the defect rate has doubled in the past month. You’re able to use your process telemetry and slew of agents to figure out that tolerances during step 7 have blown out of the acceptable range. You haven’t changed anything about your process, so you have no idea what could be causing this. Four different precursors enter the process during step 7, but those haven’t changed either.

With the help of your ASI helper, you’re able to narrow down the possible causes of this specific kind of defect to inclusion of impurity X in material Y, but both precursors A and B contain Y. You reach out to the suppliers, but they shrug and say “sorry we haven’t changed anything”, so you need to diagnose which of these is the ultimate source. You order some tests on your new stock and the remnants of the old stock, and you find out that precursor A is causing your defect.

And now you have a decision to make: do you try to find a new supplier, remove the impurity yourself, or compensate for the impurity in other ways? You’ll need to run the tests on the new material or make a purification system or change your design. These all have tradeoffs and ASI will be able to help with all of these and pick the right one, but the fundamental problem here is that it takes time and money to install new systems to fix this problem. There is the time it takes to order new components, assemble them, install them. If you are integrating it into your telemetry system, you need all the sensors and wiring to feed into some database, and then finally you need to get your production up and running and make sure it’s all working.

The crux of AI disruption in my mind is these new bottlenecks which can be roughly split into two categories:

1. What are the speed limits in the world that intelligence does not accelerate?

The purely physical speed limits in the above example are things like sending out complicated tests to be run, ordering new components, installing new hardware into your factory, and manufacturing new widgets to verify your problem has been solved. There is a practical limit to how fast you can ship things across the country, and manufacturing steps involving chemical and biological processes have fundamental rates that can be on the order of days for things like culturing human cells and annealing metals.

Now suppose you also have humanoid robots to run your factory and install the new components, handling every step along the way. A very nontrivial percentage of the time in the above example is just dealing with the other companies, sending out materials for testing, having the new parts shipped to you, and installing the physical hardware and stress-testing it. This whole process could take a month in a current factory without superintelligence, but getting a 4x speedup to ~1 week seems about as fast as you can possibly go even with omniscient machines making perfect decisions at every step and working 24/7. At some point you’re quite literally bottlenecked on shipping time and physical throughput rate of tools in your factory.

There are also problems which are more or less solved - the steam engine has been around for 300 years, yet even fusion plants will likely end up turning a steam turbine. How many other problems in the world are in some sense solved and are very slow, expensive, and boring to improve? Other speed limits in the world are less physical but still important. What is the speed of regulation? What is the speed of political will?

It is worth disambiguating speedup and scale-up here. In something like the oil industry, a multitrillion dollar industry with enormous incentive to rapidly automate, it seems even a 3x speedup would be difficult. The oil comes out of the ground at some rate, is refined at some rate, and is transported at some rate, so the obvious answer if you want to double production is to parallelize everything and just have twice as much infrastructure. But massively expanding capacity in parallelization is itself a process that can be bottlenecked. Over the last year, strange scaling bottlenecks have looked like the monocrystalline turbine blades for natural gas plants and indium phosphide wafers for optical interconnects, and this has just been for running computers. If you believe in true industrial explosions, the demand for niche magnets and bearings and sensors and tool tips and alloys will explode, and any one of them can become the rate limiter.

2. What does it actually mean to be superintelligent in the presence of noise?

The more abstract speedup question is something like “could a superintelligence, given all the context of the situation, know right away that impurity X was the culprit and that it came from precursor A?” This would save you the time you spent running tests on A versus B and let you go straight to problem solving, but is this even possible? After all, the only thing that changed was the error bar in step 7.

In the aphorism “intelligence is compression”, there is a natural next question: What is the maximum amount of compression you can achieve in the real world? In order to realize that precursor A and not B had the impurity, you need to acquire 1 bit of information. Some bits, however, are unbelievably expensive to obtain and create a similar kind of Amdahl calculus. If key bits are orders of magnitude more expensive and slower to acquire (say, for example, long-term side effect analysis of new drugs on actual humans), these will set your overall rate.

It seems most people in AI consider the world to be far less noisy than it actually is because they mostly live in a world of flawlessly repeatable execution at staggering scale. Scaling experiments is as simple as spinning up more Docker containers, but the notion of superintelligence in domains like biology is ill-defined: There are large variations between nominally identical experiments, and the rate at which experiments produce informative bits is unfathomably low compared to anything in ML or verifiable like math. In other words, even information theory-optimal exploration of some problem landscape could be agonizingly slow if experiments are slow or noisy, let alone both. (To those who believe AI would be able to simulate any process accurately enough, it’s worth appreciating how poorly understood many multi-scale interactions are and how ground truth experimentation is often your best option. See also my blog post from April.)

Outlook

Intelligence is far from the only technology curve to go quasi-infinite in the last century and a half: The world electrified. The cost of communication has gone from couriers and weeks to ~free and gigabytes per second. Computers have made calculations which were once infeasible executable on a cheap computer near-instantly. Transportation costs have fallen by an order of magnitude. From 1880 to 2026, the share of the US workforce in agriculture fell from 51% to 1.2% as we were freed to work in other fields.

Yet through it all, we’ve seen nearly 150 years of 2% GDP per capita growth. These are all general-purpose technologies, so what needs to give for ASI to be that different?




Discuss

item.title: Embryo selection and economic discounting
item.description:
My wife and I are planning to have children soon, and we will be using embryo selection to improve our family’s future well-being. Basically, the idea is that we can take a small sample of cells from each embryo, analyze their DNA, and use the genetic information to help choose which embryos we want to implant.

These days, polygenic scores are good at predicting risk for a lot of diseases, like cancer, heart disease, diabetes, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s. And companies like Herasight or Genomic Prediction often give an “embryo health score”[1] that takes an average of the predicted risk for each disease, weighted by how bad each disease is.

But how are those weights calculated? And can we do better?

Disability-adjusted life years

Diseases are bad in two ways: they can make you die, and they can make your life worse. The “disability-adjusted life year” (DALY) metric captures both of these, by combining years of life lost and years of reduced quality of life (using a factor between 0 and 1 to account for different subjective severity of disease states).[2]

Embryo selection companies, who compute polygenic scores for many different diseases, can add up the DALY burden of all the disease predictions for a given embryo. This gives an overall “embryo health score” that is a composite of these predictions.

A note on pleiotropy

Interestingly, many negative traits are genetically correlated with each other, so selecting against one selects against many. For example, our embryos that had a high schizophrenia risk also tended to have a high risk of bipolar. Pleiotropy (where one variant affects multiple traits) is often brought up in objections to embryo selection, e.g. “if you select for IQ, you might be selecting against health”, but in practice, mutations that make embryos less healthy will also generally hurt other traits.

Which diseases will be relevant in the future?

From as far back as 1950 until today, heart disease has been the biggest killer in the USA. And the DALY scores for embryos reflect this: heart disease has a strong weight.

But if a boy is born in 2027 with a high lifetime risk, he likely won’t develop any problems until middle age. Heart disease treatment will likely look very different in 2072! Therefore, we need to take into account future medical progress when weighing the badness of different diseases:

  • First, some things are already easily treatable. Statins lower cholesterol, and there are plenty of good medications for blood pressure. More recently, GLP1 drugs have made type 2 diabetes much less relevant. Some of these drugs are expensive today, but they will be generic in the future, and likely cheap and accessible.
  • On the other limb bud, any disease that is developmental in origin will not be treatable except by replacement of the affected structure. If something doesn’t form properly in the fetus, giving a drug to the adult won’t help.
  • However, organ replacement will probably be an option in 10-30 years, depending on the organ. This could include xenotransplantation or lab-grown “applied developmental biology” approaches. So things like heart disease and kidney disease will be curable, though this may be very expensive.
  • But nobody can get brain transplants.[3] Anything that affects the brain (depression, mental illness, neurodegeneration) will still be a huge problem. Very advanced technology may be able to replace the brain neuron-by-neuron, but I expect this to have the least progress compared to other diseases. Conditions that affect photoreception (e.g. colorblindness) will also be difficult to treat.
  • Cancer and autoimmune conditions are also not treatable with transplants, though emerging technologies will make treatment somewhat better.

Overall, I expect rapid medical progress in most areas over the next 50 years, especially given ongoing advances in AI. And if there’s a technological singularity, and everyone uploads their minds to run on silicon, then mental illnesses and personality disorders are the only thing that will matter!

Economic discounting

Leaving aside which conditions will be treatable in the future, the fact that some conditions have later average age of onset than others means that DALYs need to be adjusted for time-preference. For example, schizophrenia usually begins in early adulthood, whereas Alzheimer’s is a disease of old age. Selection for intelligence would have benefits at all stages of life.[4]

Embryo selection companies don’t take time-discounting into account for their embryo health scores.[5] However, health economists (e.g. in a study sponsored by the Gates Foundation) typically use a 3% annual discount rate. Personally, I think a 3% rate is on the low side: money invested today (instead of spent on embryo selection) would likely grow faster than that, especially given AI progress, and could be used to treat health conditions later in life. But I’ll use 3% in this post. Applied to the question of embryo selection, economic discounting means that late-onset conditions should be weighted less.

DALY adjustments

These are Herasight’s DALY numbers,[6] adjusted for 3% economic discounting, and further adjusted for future medical progress. I assume negligible progress in mental and neurological disorders, moderate progress in cancer and autoimmune, and faster progress in other categories (especially ones which are related to obesity/metabolic dysfunction).

Even after discounting, embryo selection is still worth it

For couples doing IVF, embryo selection (PGT) costs vary by provider but are often in the range of $500 per embryo.[7] IVF itself is much more expensive: we paid about $7500 per cycle at CNY, including costs of medication and travel, and other clinics are even more expensive. Side effects of hormone stimulation for egg retrieval also take a toll: based on my wife’s experience, I estimate that these side effects cause a loss of 0.025 DALY per IVF cycle.[8]

But all this is still much less expensive than the diseases that selection can prevent. As of 2026, one DALY is valued by the US government (HHS) as:

$726,000 … for analyses using a 3% discount rate, and $1,205,000 for analyses using a 7% discount rate[9]

Other US healthcare organizations place lower values on DALYs, often around $200,000. The difference is because the HHS number measures what people will pay to reduce their own risk of death, but other organizations are measuring cost-effectiveness of medical interventions relative to current treatment options.

The top embryo from our first IVF cycle had a non-discounted DALY gain of +1.35 years, and estimated IQ gain of +10 points, relative to our family average. Economic discounting and medical progress would shrink the DALY gain to +0.18 years, but this is still a gain of $133,000 for health and $151,000 for IQ, much more than we paid for the IVF and selection.

Of course we can’t be sure that our top embryo will successfully implant and develop to term, so we need to scale these numbers down to account for the chance we need to use our second-best or lower ranked embryos instead. In the end, being able to choose among the five embryos from our first cycle, rather than transferring them in random order, has an expected value of about $112,000.

Additional cycles run into diminishing returns, but I calculated that this point is reached for our family after 6 - 8 cycles.

Here, the optimal number of cycles is calculated as expected benefit (from health only, or health + IQ) with current Herasight predictors, minus the expected cost (direct financial cost and DALYs lost from IVF medication side effects).[10]

Our family is different from a typical family in several ways, including higher genetic risk of bipolar and schizophrenia, and younger than average age for IVF patients (meaning more embryos per cycle).

For typical families, embryo selection for health is worth it only at the highest estimates of DALY values. However, the picture changes when also considering IQ selection: typical families would come out ahead from doing at least 3 rounds of IVF, and interestingly, lower value placed on DALYs increases the optimal IVF cycle number, because the DALY cost of medication side effects becomes less relevant.

Conclusions

Given rate of progress in medicine, and economic growth, embryo selection to prevent early-onset disease is more important than selection to prevent late-onset disease. Prospective parents who are considering embryo selection should take this into account. Even with discounting, embryo selection for health+IQ still passes the cost-benefit analysis for most couples.
